notes.b: A cultural region is an area where people share one or more cultural traits that set them apart from neighbouring areas. Language and religion are the traits the syllabus uses to define them.
points: Culture is the shared way of life of a group: its language, religion, customs, music, sport and sense of identity (feeling that you belong to that group).
Language and religion are the two cultural traits the syllabus uses. Both are easy to map because census data (the official count of the population, taken every few years) records them.

Cultural regions rarely match political borders (the lines between states). One state can contain several, as Belgium and Switzerland do, and one region can cross several states, as the Basque Country and the Islamic world do.
Their edges are usually transition zones, where the shared trait gradually thins out rather than stopping at a line, because people and customs mix across any boundary.
notes.tip: If asked to define a cultural region, say it is a region where people share common traits such as language, religion and traditions.

notes.b: The Gaeltacht is the officially recognised area where Irish is, or was, the community language (the language people use in everyday life). It is not one continuous region.
points: It lies in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.

Main areas: Gaoth Dobhair (Gweedore), Co. Donegal; Conamara and the Aran Islands (Oileáin Árann), Co. Galway, the largest Gaeltacht area; Corca Dhuibhne (the Dingle Peninsula), Co. Kerry; Múscraí and Oileán Chléire (Cape Clear), Co. Cork; An Rinn (Ring), Co. Waterford; Ráth Chairn and Baile Ghib, Co. Meath.
The pockets are scattered, mainly along the western seaboard (the Atlantic coast), rather than joined into one block.

Remote, mountainous areas with poor farmland and poor communications (roads and transport links) had the least contact with English-speaking trade, towns and administration, which is why Irish survived there.

The Gaeltacht therefore overlaps with the peripheral West of Ireland (the outlying, less developed area far from the main centres of population and wealth). There is more on this in the socio-economic regions subsection.
The State created a cultural region deliberately: the two Meath Gaeltachtaí (Gaeltacht areas) were formed in the 1930s by resettling Irish-speaking families from Connemara, Ráth Chairn among them.
notes.tip: The Gaeltacht, and Dingle as part of it, is the cultural region in Ireland defined by language. Remember it is a cultural region, so it is not the same thing as a peripheral region.

notes.h: Support for the Gaeltacht and threats to it
notes.b: The State backs the Irish language with laws, institutions and media, because the Gaeltacht is small and under pressure. Several trends still threaten it.
points: Irish is the first official language under Article 8 of the 1937 Constitution, which gives the language legal standing.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, set up in 1980, promotes employment and the language in the Gaeltacht, so that people have jobs and can stay in their communities.
Raidió na Gaeltachta (1972) and TG4 (first broadcast in 1996 as Teilifís na Gaeilge) broadcast in Irish, so people can hear and watch their language daily.
State language policy is also set out in the Official Languages Act 2003.
Irish-medium schools (where lessons are taught in Irish) and summer colleges bring learners into the Gaeltacht and sustain the language there.
Threats: out-migration of young people (leaving to find work), in-migration of English speakers and holiday homes, and English-language media and tourism, all of which bring English into daily life.

Census 2022 (whole State): about 1.9 million people said they could speak Irish, but only about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system. This shows a big gap between ability and everyday use.
The Gaeltacht has shrunk and been redrawn since 1850, so its boundaries have changed. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
notes.tip: Use only the national Irish-speaker figures from Census 2022 given here. Do not quote Gaeltacht-only figures or older census figures.

notes.b: Belgium is split by a language border that runs east to west across the country, creating three language areas and a bilingual capital.
points: Flanders, in the north: Dutch-speaking. Flemish is the Dutch spoken in Flanders.
Wallonia, in the south: French-speaking, because it lies on the Latin-speaking side of the border.
A small German-speaking community in the east, around Eupen, so Belgium has three language areas in all.
The Brussels-Capital Region is officially bilingual (French and Dutch). It lies inside Flanders but is mostly French-speaking.
The border marks the old boundary between Germanic-speaking and Latin-speaking peoples (the two language families of northern and southern Europe), and was fixed by law in 1962–63.
More than half of Belgians live in Flanders.
notes.tip: Brussels lies geographically inside Flanders, so never call it part of Wallonia. Flemish is the Dutch spoken in Belgium, so do not describe it as an unrelated language.

notes.h: Political and social effects of the language divide in Belgium
notes.b: Because the two main language groups live in separate areas, language shapes how Belgium is governed and how its people live. It also lines up with a difference in wealth.
points: Belgium became a federal state in 1993, which means power is shared between a central government and regional and community governments.
It has three regions (Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels-Capital) and three language communities (Flemish, French, German-speaking), each with its own parliament.
Schools, media and political parties are divided by language, so the two main groups have separate public lives.
In 1968 the university at Leuven split: its French-speaking section moved to a new town, Louvain-la-Neuve, in Wallonia.
After the 2010 election Belgium went 541 days without a new government, because Flemish and French-speaking parties could not agree.

The language divide matches an economic divide: Flanders, with the port of Antwerp and newer industries, became the wealthier region, and many Flemish people resent money transferred to Wallonia, whose coal and steel industries in the Sambre–Meuse valley declined.
notes.tip: A full answer on Belgium gives the language areas, then specific facts such as 1993, 1968 and the 541 days, each with its date or figure.

notes.b: Several other European regions are defined mainly by language. Exams use them in matching questions, so know what marks each one out.
points: The Basque Country (Euskara): Basque is unrelated to any other European language, and the region crosses the border of Spain and France, so one cultural region lies in two states.
Catalonia, north-east Spain: Catalan is the language and Barcelona is the capital. An unofficial independence referendum (a public vote on breaking away from Spain) was held there on 1 October 2017.
Wales (Welsh) and Brittany (Breton) are Celtic-language regions, so each is defined by a Celtic language such as Welsh or Breton.
Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh, so it holds several language regions within one state.
notes.tip: The Basque Country, Catalonia, the Gaeltacht, Dingle and the Islamic world are cultural regions. The Mezzogiorno is not: it is a peripheral region.

notes.b: Religion divides Ireland in two ways. In the Republic it is changing as the Catholic share falls, and in Northern Ireland it is tied to politics and to where people live.
points: The Republic is mainly Roman Catholic, but in Census 2022 about 69% were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in Census 2016.
About 14% said they had no religion in Census 2022, and that share is rising.
Immigration has added other religions, such as Orthodox Christians and Muslims, because people bring their faith with them.
The Plantation of Ulster (the settling of Ulster with colonists), begun in 1609, brought Protestant settlers from Britain and created a Protestant majority in much of the north-east of Ulster.
Religion became tied to political identity: mostly Catholic nationalists (who want a united Ireland) and mostly Protestant unionists (who want to stay in the United Kingdom).
In Belfast, religion defines segregated residential areas, separated in places by peace walls (peace lines), barriers built between the neighbourhoods.
Census 2021 showed, for the first time, more Catholics than Protestants in Northern Ireland.
The partition (the division of Ireland), the Troubles and the Good Friday Agreement shaped this situation. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
notes.tip: Do not say Catholics are a majority in Northern Ireland. Census 2021 showed them as the largest group, not over half. Give no percentages for Northern Ireland.

notes.h: The Islamic world: origin and extent
notes.b: The Islamic world is a region defined by religion that stretches from Morocco to Indonesia. To explain it, you need to know where Islam began, how far it reaches and how it spread.
points: Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad in Arabia in the 7th century. Mecca and Medina, in present-day Saudi Arabia, are its holiest cities.
The Islamic calendar begins with the Hijra, Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina, in 622.
The Islamic world stretches from Morocco in North Africa, through the Middle East and Central Asia, to Pakistan, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country, so Islam is not confined to the Arab world.
Muslims are almost a quarter of the world's population, so Islam is the second-largest religion after Christianity.

Arab conquest carried Islam across North Africa and into Spain, beginning in 711; trade routes carried it to South and South-East Asia; the Ottoman Turks later carried it into the Balkans (the region of south-east Europe).
notes.tip: Do not equate Arab with Muslim: most Muslims live in Asia, in places such as Indonesia, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Say Muslims are almost a quarter of the world's population rather than giving a number.

notes.h: What makes the Islamic world a region
notes.b: A religion makes a region when shared beliefs and practices leave visible and lasting marks on the lives and landscape of the people. In the Islamic world these are the following.
points: A shared faith built on the Five Pillars (the five duties of a Muslim): declaration of faith; prayer five times a day, facing Mecca; giving to charity; fasting in Ramadan; and the pilgrimage to Mecca (the Hajj).
Arabic is the language of the Qur'an (the holy book of Islam), read across the region, so it unites people who speak different everyday languages.
Mosques (places of worship) and minarets (the towers beside them) mark the landscape.
Islamic law (Sharia) shapes the laws of some states, so religion affects government as well as worship.
Shared customs of dress, food and calendar, such as the Islamic calendar that begins with the Hijra, make everyday life similar across the region.
Sunni Muslims are the large majority overall. Shia Muslims are the majority in Iran and Iraq, and rivalry between the two branches of Islam adds to conflict in the Middle East.
notes.tip: When asked how religion defines a region, give specific features such as the Five Pillars, Arabic, mosques and Sharia, not just the word faith.

notes.h: Boundary zones of the Islamic world
notes.b: The edges of the Islamic world are not fixed. History and migration have left Muslim communities beyond its core, and in some places Muslim rule has ended.
points: Ottoman rule (rule by the Ottoman Turks) left Muslim communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania and Kosovo, in the Balkans.
Spain was under Muslim (Moorish) rule until Granada fell to the Christian kingdoms in 1492.
Migration has created large Muslim communities in western Europe: North Africans in France, Turks in Germany, and Pakistanis and Bangladeshis in Britain.

notes.b: Europe divides into three broad Christian regions. Each has its roots in a split within the Church, and the divisions have sometimes led to conflict.
points: Roman Catholic south and centre: Italy, Spain, Portugal, Poland, Ireland and southern Germany.
Protestant north, so a region shaped by the Reformation: Scandinavia, northern Germany and Britain.
Orthodox east and south-east: Greece, Russia, Romania and Serbia.
The Catholic and Orthodox churches split, which is why Europe has two eastern and western Christian traditions, with Rome and Constantinople at the centre of the two traditions.
The Protestant Reformation (the movement that broke away from the Catholic Church) began in Germany in 1517, with Martin Luther. Vatican City, in Rome, is the centre of the Catholic Church.
The break-up of Yugoslavia in the 1990s set Orthodox Serbs, Catholic Croats and Muslim Bosniaks against each other in war in Bosnia, showing how religious differences can fuel conflict.
notes.tip: For a 30-mark question on how culture defines regions, give a definition, then the Gaeltacht, Belgium and the Islamic world or the Irish religious regions, each with specific facts.

Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina in 622, from which the Islamic calendar begins.

Belgium is divided into Dutch-speaking Flanders in the north, French-speaking Wallonia in the south, a German-speaking community in the east, and a bilingual Brussels-Capital Region that lies inside Flanders but is mostly French-speaking. questions.prompt: Name two language regions in Belgium and state the language spoken in each.
